blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Solution: A homogeneous mixture composed of two or more substances, typically containing a solvent and one or more solutes.
  • Components: The solvent dissolves the solute and is generally present in a larger amount.
  • Dilute Solution: A solution in which relatively a small amount of solute is dissolved in large amount of solvent is called a dilute solution.
  • Concentrated Solution: A solution in which relatively a large amount of the solute is present in the given amount of solvent is called a concentrated solution.
  • Solutions can be categorized by the physical state of the solvent: gaseous, aqueous (liquid), solid, etc.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Concentration ($C$):
$C=\frac{n}{V(L)}$

Explanation: $n$ represents the number of moles of solute, and $V$ is the volume (in litre) of the solution. This formula assumes ideal behavior where interactions between molecules do not affect concentration.

blocks.title: Solutions
blocks.text: Solutions can be categorized by the physical state of the solvent: gaseous, aqueous (liquid), solid, etc.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: Calculate the concentration of a solution containing 2 moles of solute in a 4 L solution.
blocks.prompt: Calculate the concentration of a solution containing 2 moles of solute in a 4 L solution.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misconception 1: Confusing solvent with solute. The solvent is always in larger quantity.
  • Misconception 2: Assuming all solutions are liquids; solutions can also exist in gaseous and solid states.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Concentration refers to the amount of solute in a quantity of solvent or solution, crucial for determining solution properties.

Common units include:Molarity

  • Molality
  • Normality
  • Mole Fraction
  • Concentration in terms of percentage
  • Parts Per Million (ppm)
  • Volume strength of $H_2O_2$solution
Each unit is useful under different conditions.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Molarity (M):

$M=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}(lit.)}$

  • Used in volumetric reactions.
  • Temperature-dependent.
Molality (m):

$m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent (kg)}}$

  • Temperature-independent.
  • Used in boiling point elevation/freezing point depression.
Normality (N):

$N=\frac{\text{equivalents of solute}}{\text{volume of solution (lit)}}$

  • Specific to acid-base and redox reactions.
Relation between M &  N:

$N = M \times n$

• where n = n-factor

Mole Fraction (X):

$X_{\text{solute}} = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solute}} + n_{\text{solvent}}}    ,    X_{\text{solvent}} = \frac{n_{\text{solvent}}}{n_{\text{solute}} + n_{\text{solvent}}}

$

$X_{\text{solute}} + X_{\text{solvent}} = 1$

Concentration in terms of percentage:

$\text{Mass percent} = \left( \frac{\text{Weight of solute (gm)}}{\text{Weight of solution (gm)}} \right) \times 100$

$\text{Volume percent} = \left( \frac{\text{Volume of solute (mL)}}{\text{Volume of solution (mL)}} \right) \times 100$

$\text{Mass/Volume percent} = \left( \frac{\text{Weight of solute (gm)}}{\text{Volume of solution (mL)}} \right) \times 100$

Parts Per Million (ppm):

$\text{ppm (by mass)} = \left( \frac{\text{Mass of solute (g)}}{\text{Mass of solution (g)}} \right) \times 10^6$

$\text{ppm (by volume)} = \left( \frac{\text{Volume of solute (mL)}}{\text{Volume of solution (mL)}} \right) \times 10^6$

$\text{ppm(byW/V)} = \left( \frac{w \, \text{(mass of solute, g)}}{V \, \text{(volume of solution, mL)}} \right) \times 10^6$

Concept of Dilution:

$N_1 V_1 = N_2 V_2 \quad \text{and} \quad M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2$

Concept of Mixing:

$\text{Normality of }  \text{ in Resultant Solution:} $

$\quad N_1 V_1 + N_2 V_2 = N_r V_r$

  • Used in vapour pressure and colligative properties.

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
• Molarity changes with temperature.

  • Molality does not change with temperature.

blocks.title: Representation of Terms
blocks.text:
In questions terms often represent :-

    • 2M = 2 moles of Solute present in 1L Solution.
    • 2N = 2  Gram Equivalents of Solute present in 1L Solution.
    • 2m =  2 moles of Solute present in 1kg Solvent.
    • 2.3% $\frac{w}{W}$ = 2.3 g of solute present in 100 g solution.

• 2.3% $\frac{v}{V}$ = 2.3 ml of solute present in 100 ml solution.

• 2.3% $\frac{w}{V}$ = 2.3 g of solute present in 100 ml solution.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their identity.

Key properties include:

  • Relative lowering in vapor pressure
  • Elevation in boiling point
  • Depression in Freezing point
  • Osmotic pressure

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Relative Lowering in Vapour Pressure

  • Formula: $ \frac{P_0 - P}{P_0} = X_{\text{solute}}
$
  • Explanation:
  • $\mathrm{P_0}$​ is the vapor pressure of the pure solvent.
  • P is the vapor pressure of the solution.
  • $X_{\text{solute}}$: Mole fraction of solute.
Elevation in Boiling Point  & Depression in Freezing Point

Formulas:

  • Boiling Point Elevation: $\Delta T_b= K_b\cdot m$
  • Freezing Point Depression: $\Delta T_f= K_f\cdot m$
$K_b$: Ebullioscopic constant

$K_f$: Cryoscopic constant

$m$: Molality

$K_b =0.52$ $k - kg - mo{l^{ - 1}}$ (for water as a solvent)

$K_f=1.86$ $k - kg - mo{l^{ - 1}}$  (for water as a solvent)

Osmotic Pressure

  • Formula: $\Pi= M\cdot R\cdot T$
$M$: Molarity

$R$: Gas constant = 0.0821 L-atm/mol-K

$T$: Temperature in Kelvin

  • Solutions having same osmotic pressure are called Isotonic solution.
  • $\pi_1 = \pi_2$
$C_1 RT = C_2 RT$

$C_1 = C_2$ (same temperature)

$\frac{n_1}{V_1} = \frac{n_2}{V_2}$

  • Reverse Osmosis: If external pressure greater than osmotic pressure is applied, the flow of solvent molecules can be made to proceed from solution towards pure solvent, i.e., in reverse direction of the ordinary osmosis.
Reverse osmosis is used for the desalination of sea water for getting fresh drinking water.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Raoult's Law:

  • The partial vapour pressure of a component in a solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction.
Deviations from Raoult's Law:

  • Occur when interactions between different molecules are either stronger or weaker than those between similar molecules.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Raoult's Law:

  • $P_A \propto X_A \text { so } P_A=P_A{ }^0 X_A$
  • $P_B \propto X_B \text { so } P_B=P_B{ }^0 X_B$
  • $P_S=P_A{ }^0+X_B\left(P_B{ }^0-P_A{ }^0\right)$
Dalton’s Law:

  • $P_A{ }^0 X_A=Y_A P_T$ $$
  • $P_B^0 X_B=Y_B P_T$
$Y_A \text { and } Y_B $ gives mole fraction in vapour phase

$X_A \text { and } X_B $ gives mole fraction in liquid phase

Ideal Solutions:

  • Follow Raoult's Law precisely with no enthalpy change upon mixing.
  • Linear graph of vapor pressure vs. mole fraction.
  • A-A interactions = B-B inetractions = A-B interactions
  • $\Delta {{\text {V}}_{{\text {mix }}}} = 0,{\text { }}\Delta {{\text {H}}_{{\text {mix }}}} = 0$
  • Observed VP = Calculated VP
  • Observed BP = Calculated BP
  • $\Delta S_\text{mix }>0, \Delta \mathrm{G}<0$
Non-ideal Solutions:

  • Positive Deviations: $P_{\text{solution}} > P_{\text{predicted}}$
In these solutions A-B interactions are less than A-A and B-B molecular interactions.

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{V}_{\operatorname{mix}}>0 \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\operatorname{mix}}>0 \end{aligned}$

$\Delta S_{\text {mix }}=+v e, \Delta G=-v e$

  • Negative Deviations: $P_{\text{solution}} < P_{\text{predicted}}$
In these solutions the A-B interactions are stronger than the A-A and B-B molecular interactions.

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{V}_{\text {mix }}<0, \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {mix }}<0 \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:

  • Misapplying Raoult's Law to non-ideal solutions without considering deviations.

blocks.title: Additional Guidelines
blocks.text:
• Acronym: P-N-P (Positive - Non-ideal - Positive deviation) represents solutions with weaker interactions.
  • NEET Tip: For ideal solutions, remember the linear relationship in the vapor pressure vs. mole fraction graph.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Some liquids on mixing form azeotropes which are binary mixtures having the same composition in liquid and vapor phase and boil at a constant temperature.
  • The liquid and vapor have the same composition and no further separation occurs.
  • Components forming azeotrope can't be separated by fractional distillation but can be separated by azeotropic distillation.

blocks.title: Types of Azeotropes
blocks.text:
• Minimum Boiling Azeotropes: Boil at a lower temperature than either of their constituents (e.g., ethanol-water).
  • Maximum Boiling Azeotropes: Boil at a higher temperature than their constituents (e.g., hydrochloric acid-water).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
In distillation, why is it difficult to separate components of an azeotropic mixture?

(1) The components of the mixture have similar boiling points.
(2) The components of the mixture form a solution with a constant boiling point.
(3) The components of the mixture are chemically bonded.
(4) The components of the mixture do not vaporize at all.
options: (1) The components of the mixture have similar boiling points.
(2) The components of the mixture form a solution with a constant boiling point.
(3) The components of the mixture are chemically bonded.
(4) The components of the mixture do not vaporize at all.
blocks.prompt: In distillation, why is it difficult to separate components of an azeotropic mixture?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
An ideal binary mixture of acetone and chloroform forms an azeotrope. At what condition does this azeotrope occur?

(1) The vapor composition is richer in acetone than the liquid composition.
(2) The liquid composition is richer in acetone than the vapor composition.
(3) The vapor composition is identical to the liquid composition.
(4) The liquid and vapor compositions are the same as pure acetone.
options: (1) The vapor composition is richer in acetone than the liquid composition.
(2) The liquid composition is richer in acetone than the vapor composition.
(3) The vapor composition is identical to the liquid composition.
(4) The liquid and vapor compositions are the same as pure acetone.
blocks.prompt: An ideal binary mixture of acetone and chloroform forms an azeotrope. At what condition does this azeotrope occur?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text: Assuming azeotropes can be separated by distillation like regular mixtures.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Henry's Law: The partial pressure of the gas is proportional to the mole fraction of a gas . This law is applicable to:

  • Dilute solutions
  • Non-reactive gases
Solubility of Gases in Liquid: Certain gases are highly soluble in water like $NH_3$, HCl etc. and certain gases are less soluble in water like $O_2, N_2$, He etc.

  • Solubility of gases is affected by pressure and temperature.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Henry’s Law Formula: $P=K_H \cdot X$
  • Variables:
$P$: Partial pressure of gas (atm)

$K_H$: Henry's Law constant (varies with gas, solvent, temperature)

$X$: mole fraction of gas (unitless) or Solubility

  • Conditions & Limitations:
Valid for dilute solutions, non-reactive gases, and when there is no chemical reaction between the gas and the solvent.

blocks.title: DATA
blocks.text:
Henry's Law:

$T\uparrow  ,  K_H\uparrow  , Solubility(X)\downarrow$

  • $K_H $ is not a universal constant. It depends on temperature.
  • Those gases which can react with solvent do not follow Henry's Law. e.g. $NH_3$in water.
Solubility of Gases in Liquid:

$T\uparrow    Solubility\downarrow  ,  P\uparrow    Solubility\uparrow $

  • During dissolution of gas pressure of gas decrease and its dissolution is also exothermic in nature.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: A solution where the mole fraction of oxygen ($O_2$​) in water is 0.0015 at a temperature where the Henry's Law constant for $O_2$​ in water is 1.3 × 10⁻³ atm. What is the partial pressure of ($O_2$​) above the solution?
blocks.prompt: A solution where the mole fraction of oxygen ($O_2$​) in water is 0.0015 at a temperature where the Henry's Law constant for $O_2$​ in water is 1.3 × 10⁻³ atm. What is the partial pressure of ($O_2$​) above the solution?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misinterpreting $k_H$: Remember, a smaller $k_H$ means greater solubility.
  • Assuming universal applicability of Henry's Law without considering its conditions and limitations.

modules.name: Van't Hoff Factor and Abnormal Colligative Properties

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Van't Hoff Factor ($i$):

  • Indicates the degree of dissociation or association of solute particles in a solution.
  • Affects colligative properties by altering expected values.
Abnormal Colligative Properties:

Deviations from expected values occur due to:

  • Solute dissociation (more particles).
  • Solute association (fewer particles).

blocks.title: DATA
blocks.text:
Constants:

  • $K_b$: ebullioscopic constant.
  • $K_f$: cryoscopic constant.
  • $R$: universal gas constant = 0.0821 L-atm/mol-K
  • $T$: temperature in Kelvin.
  • $M$: molarity.
  • $m$: molality.
$K_b =0.52$ $k - kg - mo{l^{ - 1}}$ (for water as a solvent)

$K_f =1.86$ $k - kg - mo{l^{ - 1}}$ (for water as a solvent)

blocks.title: Formula and Mathematical Problems
blocks.text:
Van't Hoff factor ($i$):

$i=\frac{\text{number of particles after dissociation or association}}{\text{number of particles before dissociation or association}}$

$i=\frac{\text{(observed/experimental/abnormal)colligative properties}}{\text{(calculated/normal) colligative properties}}$

$i=\frac{\text{(calculated/normal) molecular mass}}{\text{(observed/experimental/abnormal) molecular mass}}$.

$i=1$  (Neither dissociation nor association Ex. glucose, urea, sugar)

$i>1$ (Dissociation will occur Ex. $\mathrm{NaCl}, \mathrm{KCl}, \mathrm{BaCl}_2$)

$i<1$  (Association will occur Ex. $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}, \mathrm{PhCOOH} \text { in benzene }$)

  • C.P $\propto$ $\frac{1}{\text{molecular~mass}}$
• Dissociation of solute:

$i = 1 + (n–1)\alpha$

If $\alpha = $ 1 or 100%

then $i = n$

Where $n$ = total number of dissociate ions

• Association of solute:

$i = 1 - \alpha + \frac{\alpha}{n}$

If $\alpha =$ 1 or 100%

then $i = \frac{1}{n}$

Where $n$ = number of solute particles which are associated.

• Relationship Between Colligative Properties and Van't hoff factor

Relative lowering in vapour pressure:

$\frac{\left(P_o-P\right)}{P_0}=\mathrm{i} \times \mathrm{X}_{\text {Solute }}$

Elevation in Boiling Point

$\Delta T_b=T_b-T_b{ }^0=i \times K_b \times m$

Depression in Freezing Point:

$\Delta T_f=T_f{ }^0-T_f=i \times K_f \times m$

Osmotic Pressure:

$\pi=i \times C \times R \times T$

blocks.question: Calculate the elevation in boiling point  for a solution of NaCl with a molality of 2 $mol/kg$, given $K_b = 0.52  ^oC kg/mol$ and assuming complete dissociation.

$\text{Volume percent} = \left( \frac{\text{Volume of solute (mL)}}{\text{Volume of solution (mL)}} \right) \times 100$

$\text{Mass/Volume percent} = \left( \frac{\text{Weight of solute (gm)}}{\text{Volume of solution (mL)}} \right) \times 100$

Parts Per Million (ppm):

$\text{ppm (by mass)} = \left( \frac{\text{Mass of solute (g)}}{\text{Mass of solution (g)}} \right) \times 10^6$

$\text{ppm (by volume)} = \left( \frac{\text{Volume of solute (mL)}}{\text{Volume of solution (mL)}} \right) \times 10^6$

$\text{ppm(byW/V)} = \left( \frac{w \, \text{(mass of solute, g)}}{V \, \text{(volume of solution, mL)}} \right) \times 10^6$

Concept of Dilution:

$N_1 V_1 = N_2 V_2 \quad \text{and} \quad M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2$

Concept of Mixing:

$\text{Normality of }  \text{ in Resultant Solution:} $

$\quad N_1 V_1 + N_2 V_2 = N_r V_r$

  • Used in vapour pressure and colligative properties.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Raoult's Law:

  • $P_A \propto X_A \text { so } P_A=P_A{ }^0 X_A$
  • $P_B \propto X_B \text { so } P_B=P_B{ }^0 X_B$
  • $P_S=P_A{ }^0+X_B\left(P_B{ }^0-P_A{ }^0\right)$
Dalton’s Law:

  • $P_A{ }^0 X_A=Y_A P_T$ $$
  • $P_B^0 X_B=Y_B P_T$
$Y_A \text { and } Y_B $ gives mole fraction in vapour phase

$X_A \text { and } X_B $ gives mole fraction in liquid phase

Ideal Solutions:

  • Follow Raoult's Law precisely with no enthalpy change upon mixing.
  • Linear graph of vapor pressure vs. mole fraction.
  • A-A interactions = B-B inetractions = A-B interactions
  • $\Delta {{\text {V}}_{{\text {mix }}}} = 0,{\text { }}\Delta {{\text {H}}_{{\text {mix }}}} = 0$
  • Observed VP = Calculated VP
  • Observed BP = Calculated BP
  • $\Delta S_\text{mix }>0, \Delta \mathrm{G}<0$
Non-ideal Solutions:

  • Positive Deviations: $P_{\text{solution}} > P_{\text{predicted}}$
In these solutions A-B interactions are less than A-A and B-B molecular interactions.

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{V}_{\operatorname{mix}}>0 \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\operatorname{mix}}>0 \end{aligned}$

$\Delta S_{\text {mix }}=+v e, \Delta G=-v e$

  • Negative Deviations: $P_{\text{solution}} < P_{\text{predicted}}$
In these solutions the A-B interactions are stronger than the A-A and B-B molecular interactions.

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{V}_{\text {mix }}<0, \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {mix }}<0 \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Henry’s Law Formula: $P=K_H \cdot X$
  • Variables:
$P$: Partial pressure of gas (atm)

$K_H$: Henry's Law constant (varies with gas, solvent, temperature)

$X$: mole fraction of gas (unitless) or Solubility

  • Conditions & Limitations:
Valid for dilute solutions, non-reactive gases, and when there is no chemical reaction between the gas and the solvent.

blocks.title: DATA
blocks.text:
Constants:

  • $K_b$: ebullioscopic constant.
  • $K_f$: cryoscopic constant.
  • $R$: universal gas constant = 0.0821 L-atm/mol-K
  • $T$: temperature in Kelvin.
  • $M$: molarity.
  • $m$: molality.
$K_b =0.52$ $k - kg - mo{l^{ - 1}}$ (for water as a solvent)

$K_f =1.86$ $k - kg - mo{l^{ - 1}}$ (for water as a solvent)

blocks.title: Formula and Mathematical Problems
blocks.text:
Van't Hoff factor ($i$):

$i=\frac{\text{number of particles after dissociation or association}}{\text{number of particles before dissociation or association}}$

$i=\frac{\text{(observed/experimental/abnormal)colligative properties}}{\text{(calculated/normal) colligative properties}}$

$i=\frac{\text{(calculated/normal) molecular mass}}{\text{(observed/experimental/abnormal) molecular mass}}$.

$i=1$  (Neither dissociation nor association Ex. glucose, urea, sugar)

$i>1$ (Dissociation will occur Ex. $\mathrm{NaCl}, \mathrm{KCl}, \mathrm{BaCl}_2$)

$i<1$  (Association will occur Ex. $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}, \mathrm{PhCOOH} \text { in benzene }$)

  • C.P $\propto$ $\frac{1}{\text{molecular~mass}}$
• Dissociation of solute:

$i = 1 + (n–1)\alpha$

If $\alpha = $ 1 or 100%

then $i = n$

Where $n$ = total number of dissociate ions

• Association of solute:

$i = 1 - \alpha + \frac{\alpha}{n}$

If $\alpha =$ 1 or 100%

then $i = \frac{1}{n}$

Where $n$ = number of solute particles which are associated.

• Relationship Between Colligative Properties and Van't hoff factor

Relative lowering in vapour pressure:

$\frac{\left(P_o-P\right)}{P_0}=\mathrm{i} \times \mathrm{X}_{\text {Solute }}$

Elevation in Boiling Point

$\Delta T_b=T_b-T_b{ }^0=i \times K_b \times m$

Depression in Freezing Point:

$\Delta T_f=T_f{ }^0-T_f=i \times K_f \times m$

Osmotic Pressure:

$\pi=i \times C \times R \times T$
